module.title: 4 · Assumptions & diagnostics
module.summary: Gauss–Markov, heteroskedasticity, and robust standard errors.

stages.title: When is OLS trustworthy?
stages.html:
The fine print

OLS is unbiased when the error is mean-zero and uncorrelated with x. It is the most efficient linear unbiased estimator (Gauss–Markov) when the errors also have constant variance (homoskedasticity) and are uncorrelated.

Real data often violate constant variance — the spread of y grows with x (heteroskedasticity). OLS estimates stay unbiased, but the standard errors are wrong. The fix is robust (HC) standard errors.

stages.title: Spot heteroskedasticity, then fix the SEs
stages.note: Residuals that fan out signal heteroskedasticity; HC1 robust SEs correct the inference.
stages.code:
import numpy as np, statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0); n = 300
x = rng.uniform(0, 3, n)
y = 1 + 2 * x + rng.normal(0, 0.4 + 0.9 * x, n)   # variance grows with x

res = sm.OLS(y, sm.add_constant(x)).fit()
res_robust = res.get_robustcov_results(cov_type="HC1")
print("classical SE:", np.round(res.bse, 3))
print("robust  SE :", np.round(res_robust.bse, 3))

plt.figure(figsize=(6, 3.7))
plt.scatter(x, res.resid, s=12, color="#da9100", alpha=0.5)
plt.axhline(0, color="#c9c6ac", lw=1)
plt.xlabel("x"); plt.ylabel("residual")
plt.title("Residuals fan out → heteroskedasticity")

stages.title: Check
stages.prompt: Under heteroskedasticity, ordinary OLS gives you…
stages.hint: Heteroskedasticity is about the variance of the error, not its mean.
stages.explain: Coefficients remain unbiased; only the standard errors are wrong — use robust (HC) SEs.

stages.title: Does heteroskedasticity bias the coefficients?
stages.prompt: You just saw the residuals fan out with x. Claim: heteroskedasticity biases the OLS coefficients, so you must drop the affected observations.
stages.hint: Heteroskedasticity changes the error's variance, not its mean. Which OLS property depends on the mean of the error?
stages.explain: This is the heteroskedasticity-biases-coefficients trap. Heteroskedasticity is about the variance of the error, not its mean — so unbiasedness (which needs E[ε|x]=0) is untouched; β̂ stays unbiased and only the default standard errors are wrong. The tempting fix — deleting data — throws away valid information and introduces selection bias. Boundary: the right fix is robust (HC1) standard errors, which correct the inference while leaving the unbiased coefficients in place.

stages.title: What does heteroskedasticity actually break?
stages.prompt: Residuals fan out with x. Select all that apply: which statements about OLS under heteroskedasticity are TRUE?
choices: The coefficient estimates β̂ remain unbiased
The default (classical) standard errors are wrong
Robust (HC1) standard errors fix the inference
The coefficient estimates β̂ become biased
You should delete the high-variance observations to fix it
stages.hint: Separate what changes (the variance of the error, hence the SEs) from what doesn't (the mean of the error, hence unbiasedness).
stages.explain: This re-plants the heteroskedasticity-biases-coefficients trap as a set. TRUE: β̂ stays unbiased (it needs E[ε|x]=0, untouched by non-constant variance), the classical SEs are wrong, and robust HC1 SEs repair the inference. FALSE distractors: 'β̂ becomes biased' is the central misconception — variance is not bias; and 'delete the high-variance observations' discards valid data and induces selection bias. Boundary: heteroskedasticity costs you efficiency and correct SEs, never unbiasedness.
